definition: Adulation means excessive, gushing, often fawning praise or admiration.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word adulation. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know adulation should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The young gymnast found the adulation after her first gold medal more exhausting than the routine itself.
Praise is measured approval; adulation is praise turned up past reason, gushing and uncritical.
Worship goes one step beyond adulation — the admirer no longer just gushes but treats the person as something sacred.

Hero-worship is a lasting attitude of idolizing one person as a larger-than-life hero -- someone the admirer looks up to and tries to imitate over time. Adulation is the outpouring itself: gushing praise and admiration showered on someone, often on a single occasion. Hero-worship lives in the admirer's head; adulation spills out in public.

Fawning is over-eager, servile praise aimed at pleasing someone -- the flatterer bows and gushes to stay in a powerful person's good graces. Adulation, by contrast, is genuinely felt: the admirers gain nothing and mean every word; the praise is simply swollen far past reason. Fawning performs; adulation overflows.

a complete lack of interest
Crowds that adulate a star are fawning over her — the verb form built on the very same Latin root, adulari, 'to fawn on.'
Adulation means excessive, gushing, often fawning praise or admiration.
By the third city of her book tour, Naomi's signings had turned into something else entirely.
Readers pressed gifts into her hands, a man read aloud a poem he had written about her, and one woman burst into tears just reaching the front of the line.
Naomi smiled through the adulation, but that night she told her editor she missed being asked hard questions about the book.
The gifts, the poem, and the tears show praise swollen far past ordinary appreciation — that flood of gushing, fawning admiration is adulation.
formal; often faintly critical

Adulation is gushing and usually uncritical — more than earned renown, less official than a commendation, and unlike idolatrous devotion it names the over-the-top praise itself rather than god-like worship; note too that adulation is genuinely felt by the admirers, whereas flattery is calculated praise with an angle behind it.

When the film opened, nineteen-year-old Mara Voss became famous in a single weekend.
Strangers wept at airports when they saw her.
Fan letters arrived by the crate, many addressed simply to 'the greatest actress alive.' At first the adulation was thrilling.
Then it began to feel like weather -- constant, indiscriminate, and nothing to do with her.
The tributes never mentioned her work: the accent she had drilled for months, the scene she had rebuilt line by line with the director.
What she wanted, she told a friend, was one honest note on her acting.
What she got was applause too loud to hear anything through.
